blocks.html: In Grade 6 you found unit rates like "120 miles in 3 hours is 40 miles per hour." A unit rate answers one question: how much for 1? Now the amounts can be fractions. Walking $\frac{1}{2}$ mile in $\frac{1}{4}$ hour is a rate too, and it has a unit rate.

To find "A per 1 B," divide: $\text{A} \div \text{B}$. The quantity after the word "per" goes in the divisor. With fractions, divide the way you learned in dividing fractions: multiply by the reciprocal.

In $\frac{1}{4}$ hour you walk $\frac{1}{2}$ mile. An hour holds 4 quarter hours, so in 1 hour you walk 4 times as far: $4 \times \frac{1}{2} = 2$ miles. Multiplying both amounts by 4 keeps the rate the same and turns $\frac{1}{4}$ hour into 1 hour. That is exactly what $\frac{1}{2} \div \frac{1}{4} = \frac{1}{2} \times 4 = 2$ does.

blocks.name: g7-rateline
blocks.cap: Step along in equal batches of $\frac{1}{2}$ mile per $\frac{1}{4}$ hour. Press "1 hour" to jump to the unit rate, or "1 mile" to see the other unit rate.

blocks.title: A walking speed
blocks.q: Ana walks $\frac{1}{2}$ mile in $\frac{1}{4}$ hour. What is her speed in miles per hour?
steps: "Miles per hour" means miles for 1 hour, so hours go in the divisor: $\frac{1}{2} \div \frac{1}{4}$.
Check: at 2 miles per hour, a quarter hour covers a quarter of 2 miles, which is $\frac{1}{2}$ mile ✓.

blocks.title: A recipe rate
blocks.q: A recipe uses $\frac{3}{4}$ cup of sugar for every $\frac{1}{2}$ cup of flour. How much sugar is that per cup of flour?
steps: So each cup of flour goes with $1\frac{1}{2}$ cups of sugar. That makes sense: 1 cup of flour is two half cups, so it needs twice $\frac{3}{4}$.
blocks.a: $1\frac{1}{2}$ cups of sugar per cup of flour

blocks.title: Mixed numbers
blocks.q: A bike rider goes $2\frac{1}{2}$ miles in $\frac{3}{4}$ hour. What is the speed in miles per hour?
steps: Write the mixed number as a fraction: $2\frac{1}{2} = \frac{5}{2}$.
$\frac{10}{3} = 3\frac{1}{3}$. Estimate to check: in a bit less than 1 hour the rider went $2\frac{1}{2}$ miles, so in a full hour a bit more than that ✓.

blocks.html: Dividing the other way: $\frac{1}{4} \div \frac{1}{2} = \frac{1}{2}$. That is a real rate, but it is hours per mile (half an hour for each mile), not miles per hour. Before you divide, say the units out loud: "miles per hour" means miles $\div$ hours. A quick check: the two unit rates are reciprocals, $2$ and $\frac{1}{2}$.
You may see a rate written as a fraction of fractions, like $\dfrac{\frac{1}{2}}{\frac{1}{4}}$. It means the same division: $\frac{1}{2} \div \frac{1}{4}$.

blocks.html: You have built ratio tables: multiply both amounts by the same number and the ratio stays the same. A table like that shows a proportional relationship. Many tables look steady but are not proportional. Here is how to tell.
Two quantities are proportional when $\frac{y}{x}$ is the same number for every pair in the table. That number is the constant of proportionality.

Proportional means "scale one amount and the other scales the same way." If 2 tickets cost \$30, then 4 tickets (twice as many) cost \$60 (twice as much). This only works when every $y$ is the same multiple of its $x$, and that is the same as saying $\frac{y}{x}$ never changes. Adding a fixed amount breaks it: with $y = x + 3$, going from $x = 1$ to $x = 2$ doubles $x$ but takes $y$ from 4 to 5.

blocks.name: ratiotable
blocks.cap: Each batch uses 2 cups of flour for 5 muffins. Try "What if we add instead?" to see why adding the same amount to both does not keep the ratio.

blocks.title: A proportional table
blocks.q: Is pay proportional to hours? $$\begin{array}{l|ccc} \text{Hours} & 2 & 3 & 5 \\ \hline \text{Pay (dollars)} & 30 & 45 & 75 \end{array}$$
steps: Divide each pay by its hours: $\frac{30}{2} = 15$, $\frac{45}{3} = 15$, $\frac{75}{5} = 15$.
Every quotient is 15, so pay is proportional to hours: \$15 for each hour.

blocks.title: Steady, but not proportional
blocks.q: Is $y$ proportional to $x$? $$\begin{array}{l|cccc} x & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 \\ \hline y & 4 & 5 & 6 & 7 \end{array}$$
steps: The quotients change, so it is not proportional. Here $y$ is always $x + 3$: the table adds, it does not multiply.

blocks.html: Calling a table proportional because its values go up by the same amount each time. Steady growth is not enough. Check: divide $y$ by $x$ in at least two columns (all of them, to be sure). Another check: does $x = 0$ go with $y = 0$? For $y = x + 3$ it would go with $3$, so it is not proportional.

blocks.html: In Grade 6 you graphed ratio tables and saw the points line up toward $(0, 0)$. That picture is the test for proportional relationships, and it has two parts.
A graph shows a proportional relationship when it is a straight line (or points on one) and it passes through the origin, $(0, 0)$.

A proportional relationship is $y = kx$. Put in $x = 0$: $y = k \cdot 0 = 0$, so $(0, 0)$ is always on the graph. And each step of 1 to the right adds the same amount, $k$, to $y$, so the graph never bends. A line like $y = 2x + 3$ is straight, but it starts at $(0, 3)$, and the extra 3 breaks the "same ratio" rule.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: The blue line $f(x) = kx$ always passes through the origin; move the slider to change $k$. The dashed red line is straight but starts at $(0, 3)$, so it is not proportional.

blocks.title: Points through the origin
blocks.q: A graph shows the points $(0, 0)$, $(2, 3)$, $(4, 6)$ and $(6, 9)$ on one straight line. Is it proportional?
steps: The points line up, and the line passes through $(0, 0)$.
Check the ratios: $\frac{3}{2} = \frac{6}{4} = \frac{9}{6} = 1.5$. They match, so $y = 1.5x$.

blocks.title: Straight, but misses the origin
blocks.q: A straight line passes through $(0, 2)$ and $(3, 8)$. Is it proportional?
steps: At $x = 0$ the line is at $y = 2$, not $0$.
So it is not proportional. Check the ratio at $(3, 8)$: $\frac{8}{3}$. At a third point, $(6, 14)$, it is $\frac{14}{6} = \frac{7}{3}$. The ratios differ.

blocks.title: Through the origin, but curved
blocks.q: A square's area $A$ is graphed against its side $s$: the points $(0, 0)$, $(1, 1)$, $(2, 4)$, $(3, 9)$. Is area proportional to side length?
steps: The graph starts at the origin, but it curves upward.
$\frac{1}{1} = 1$, $\frac{4}{2} = 2$, $\frac{9}{3} = 3$: the ratio grows, so it is not proportional.

blocks.html: Accepting any straight line. A proportional graph must pass through $(0, 0)$, because zero of one quantity goes with zero of the other. Check by looking where the line crosses the $y$-axis: if it is not at $0$, the relationship is not proportional.

blocks.html: In a proportional table, $\frac{y}{x}$ is the same for every pair. That fixed number is so useful that it has a name: the constant of proportionality, usually called $k$.
$k = \frac{y}{x}$ for any pair (with $x \ne 0$). It is the unit rate: the amount of $y$ that goes with 1 of $x$.

If every $y$ is $k$ times its $x$, then dividing $y$ by $x$ undoes the multiplying and leaves $k$. And when $x = 1$, $y = k \times 1 = k$, so $k$ is "how much for 1," the same unit rate you already know.

blocks.name: ratiotable
blocks.cap: 4 pounds of apples cost \$10. Press "Unit rate" to see the price of 1 pound: that is $k = 2.5$.

blocks.title: From a table
blocks.q: $y$ is proportional to $x$. Find $k$. $$\begin{array}{l|ccc} x & 3 & 5 & 8 \\ \hline y & 12 & 20 & 32 \end{array}$$

blocks.title: From a story
blocks.q: Rosa pays \$7.50 for 3 pounds of grapes. What is the constant of proportionality, in dollars per pound?
steps: Dollars per pound means dollars $\div$ pounds: $7.50 \div 3 = 2.50$.

blocks.title: From a graph
blocks.q: A proportional graph passes through the origin and $(4, 10)$. Find $k$.
steps: Every point on the line has the same ratio, so use $(4, 10)$: $k = \frac{10}{4} = 2.5$.
The line also passes through $(1, 2.5)$, the unit rate.

blocks.html: $k$ does not have to be a whole number. It can be a fraction like $\frac{3}{4}$ or a decimal like $0.4$. It is still the amount of $y$ for each 1 of $x$.

blocks.html: Once you know the constant of proportionality, you can write the whole relationship as one short equation. It works for every row of the table at once.
A proportional relationship can be written $y = kx$, where $k = \frac{y}{x}$. Find $k$ from any pair, then write the equation.
"Proportional" means each $y$ is $k$ times its $x$. The equation $y = kx$ says exactly that. It also lets you find a $y$ for any $x$, even one that is not in the table.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Change $k$ and watch the table: every $y$-value is $k$ times its $x$-value, and the row for $x = 1$ shows $k$ itself.

blocks.title: From a table
blocks.q: $y$ is proportional to $x$. Write an equation. $$\begin{array}{l|ccc} x & 2 & 5 & 8 \\ \hline y & 7 & 17.5 & 28 \end{array}$$

blocks.title: From a story
blocks.q: 4 movie tickets cost \$34. Let $c$ be the cost in dollars and $n$ the number of tickets. Write an equation for $c$ in terms of $n$.

blocks.title: Watch the order
steps: $k = \frac{y}{x} = \frac{2}{6} = \frac{1}{3}$. Here $y$ is smaller than $x$, so $k$ is less than 1.

blocks.html: Dividing $x$ by $y$ and writing the reciprocal, like $y = 3x$ in the last example. Always check your equation with a row of the table: $3 \times 6 = 18$, not $2$, so $y = 3x$ is wrong.

blocks.html: Every point on a proportional graph tells a small story. To read it, remember what each axis measures.
A point $(x, y)$ means "$x$ of the first quantity goes with $y$ of the second." The point $(1, k)$ shows the unit rate, and $(0, 0)$ means none of one goes with none of the other.
The graph of $y = kx$ is made of all the pairs that fit the relationship. At $x = 1$ the equation gives $y = k$, so the unit rate always appears as the point $(1, k)$. At $x = 0$ it gives $y = 0$.

blocks.name: graph
blocks.cap: Maya earns \$12 an hour. Drag the point along the line: at 1 hour it reads $(1, 12)$, the unit rate.

blocks.title: Reading a point
blocks.q: Maya's pay graph (hours across, dollars up) passes through $(5, 60)$. What does that point mean?
steps: The first number is hours and the second is dollars.

blocks.title: Finding the unit rate point
blocks.q: A proportional graph of pages read (up) against minutes (across) passes through $(4, 6)$. Which point shows the unit rate?
steps: The unit rate point is $(1, 1.5)$: in 1 minute, 1.5 pages.

blocks.title: Using a point to predict
blocks.q: The same graph passes through $(4, 6)$. How many pages are read in 10 minutes?
steps: The point $(10, 15)$ is on the line.

blocks.html: Reading a point backwards. $(5, 60)$ on an hours-and-dollars graph does not mean "\$5 for 60 hours." The $x$-value always comes first. Check: does your sentence match the labels on the axes?

blocks.html: A typical problem gives three numbers from a proportional relationship and asks for the fourth: "5 notebooks cost \$8.75; how much for 7?" You already know $y = kx$ from writing equations. Here are three ways to finish the job.

Use the unit rate (find the amount for 1, then multiply), a scale factor (find what one amount was multiplied by), or cross products ($\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$ means $ad = bc$). Each works only when the relationship is proportional.

Why cross products work: start with $\frac{a}{b} = \frac{c}{d}$ and multiply both sides by $b$ and by $d$. The $b$ cancels on the left and the $d$ cancels on the right, leaving $ad = cb$. It is not a trick; it is two multiplications done to both sides at once.

blocks.cap: 2 cups of rice need 3 cups of water. How much water goes with 7 cups of rice? 7 is not a whole number of batches, so go through the unit rate.

blocks.title: Unit rate
blocks.q: 5 notebooks cost \$8.75. How much do 7 notebooks cost?

blocks.title: Scale factor
blocks.q: Solve $\frac{3}{8} = \frac{x}{40}$.
steps: The denominator went from 8 to 40: that is $\times 5$.
Do the same to the numerator: $x = 3 \times 5 = 15$.

blocks.title: Cross products
blocks.q: Solve $\frac{6}{x} = \frac{9}{12}$.

blocks.html: Two traps. Mismatched units: setting miles over gallons equal to gallons over miles. Write the units next to each number; both ratios must compare the same things in the same order. Not proportional: a plant is 4 cm tall and grows 2 cm each week. After 3 weeks it is 10 cm, and after 6 weeks it is 16 cm. The proportion $\frac{3}{10} = \frac{6}{x}$ would say 20 cm, which is wrong, because the height is not a fixed multiple of the weeks. Ask first: does doubling one amount double the other?

blocks.html: You know how to find a percent of a number and how to find the whole from a part. Percent change puts those together. It answers: compared with where we started, how big was the change?
$$\text{percent change} = \frac{\text{amount of change}}{\text{original amount}} \times 100\%$$ It is an increase when the new amount is bigger and a decrease when it is smaller.

A percent always compares a part with a whole. "By what percent did the price go up?" means "the increase is what percent of the price we started with?" So the original amount is the whole, the 100%. After an increase of 25%, the new amount is $100\% + 25\% = 125\%$ of the original.

blocks.name: percentbar
blocks.cap: A \$40 price grows to \$50. The original \$40 is 100%; the new price, \$50, is 125% of it. The \$10 increase is the extra 25%.

blocks.title: An increase
blocks.q: A video game's price went from \$40 to \$50. Find the percent increase.

blocks.title: A decrease
blocks.q: A club had 80 members last year and has 60 now. Find the percent decrease.

blocks.title: Finding the new amount
blocks.q: A \$60 coat goes up in price by 15%. What is the new price?
steps: The new price is $100\% + 15\% = 115\%$ of the old price.

blocks.html: Dividing by the new amount. For \$40 to \$50, $\frac{10}{50} = 20\%$ is wrong. Check: 20% of the original \$40 is only \$8, and $40 + 8 = 48$, not 50. Always divide by the amount you started with.
The same change can be different percents. Going from 40 to 50 is a 25% increase, but going from 50 back to 40 is a 20% decrease, because the starting amount changed.

blocks.html: Stores use percent change all the time. A discount takes a percent off; sales tax, a tip or a markup adds a percent on. One multiplication can do each job.
With $d\%$ off, you pay $(100 - d)\%$ of the price. With $t\%$ added (tax, tip or markup), you pay $(100 + t)\%$. Write that percent as a decimal and multiply.

20% off a price $p$ is $p - 0.20p$. By the distributive property that is $(1 - 0.20)p = 0.80p$: you pay 80%. In the same way, 6% tax gives $p + 0.06p = 1.06p$. When there are two changes, the second percent is taken of the new price, so you multiply twice.

blocks.q: A \$60 jacket is on sale for 20% off. What is the sale price?

steps: The coupon takes 10% off \$40, not off \$50: $0.90 \times 40 = 36$.
In one step: $50 \times 0.80 \times 0.90 = 50 \times 0.72 = 36$. You pay 72%, which is 28% off, not 30%.

blocks.html: Adding the discounts: "20% off and then 10% off is 30% off." That would give \$35, but the second discount comes off a smaller price, so it saves less. Check: 10% of \$40 is \$4, not \$5.

blocks.html: When you put money in a savings account, the bank pays you for using it. That payment is interest. With simple interest, each year you earn the same percent of the amount you put in.
$$I = Prt$$ $I$ is the interest, $P$ the principal (the money you start with), $r$ the yearly rate as a decimal, and $t$ the time in years. The balance at the end is $P + I$.

One year of interest is $r$ times the principal: $P \times r$. Simple interest pays that same amount every year, so after $t$ years you have $t$ of them: $(P \times r) \times t$. (Many real accounts pay "compound" interest, which also earns interest on old interest. You will meet that later.)

blocks.html: Estimates and measurements are rarely perfect. Percent error tells how far off they are compared with the true value. It works like percent change, with the actual value as the whole.
$$\text{percent error} = \frac{|\text{estimate} - \text{actual}|}{\text{actual}} \times 100\%$$

Being off by 2 cm on a 10 cm pencil is a big miss: 20% of its length. Being off by 2 cm on a 200 cm door is tiny: 1%. Dividing by the actual value measures the error against the size of the real thing. The absolute value bars mean we only care how far off we were, not whether we guessed too high or too low.

blocks.title: Rounding
blocks.q: An estimate of 50 people turns out to be 47. Find the percent error to the nearest tenth of a percent.
steps: That is about $6.383\%$, which rounds to $6.4\%$.

blocks.html: Maps, floor plans and models show real things at a different size. A scale such as "1 cm represents 5 m" tells how lengths on the drawing match real lengths. Every scale problem is a proportion.

Real length $=$ drawing length $\times$ the scale, and drawing length $=$ real length $\div$ the scale. Areas do not scale the same way: if lengths are multiplied by $k$, areas are multiplied by $k^2$.

A rectangle has two lengths, and both of them grow. If each side becomes $k$ times as long, the area becomes $k \times k = k^2$ times as big. On a grid you can see it: a copy at scale 2 holds $2 \times 2 = 4$ copies of the original, and at scale 3 it holds 9.

steps: Each centimeter on the map is 5 m.

steps: The wall is 4.5 cm long on the plan.

steps: Compare: the plan's area is $12$ square cm, and $12 \times 2^2 = 48$ ✓.

A scale with no units, like $1 : 50$, means real lengths are 50 times the drawing lengths, in the same units: 1 cm on the drawing is 50 cm in real life.

blocks.html: In Grade 6 you met opposites: $3$ and $-3$ are the same distance from $0$, on opposite sides. This lesson is about what happens when you add them. It is the key to adding any signed numbers.
A number plus its opposite is zero: $a + (-a) = 0$. A $+1$ and a $-1$ together make a zero pair.

Adding a positive number moves you right on the number line; adding a negative number moves you left. Start at $0$, move 5 right, then 5 left: you are back at $0$. With money it is the same: earn \$5, spend \$5, and you have the same amount as before.

steps: $6$ and $-6$ are opposites, so together they make $0$.

blocks.html: Since opposites make zero, you can add any two signed numbers. Think of each number as a move on the number line: positive moves right, negative moves left.
Same signs: add the absolute values and keep the sign. Different signs: subtract the smaller absolute value from the larger, and give the answer the sign of the number farther from $0$.

With different signs the moves go opposite ways, so part of one cancels part of the other. In $-7 + 3$, three of the seven steps left are undone by the three steps right (three zero pairs). The 4 steps left that remain give $-4$. That is why you subtract: the cancelled part disappears.

steps: The signs are different. Subtract the absolute values: $7 - 3 = 4$.
$-7$ is farther from $0$, so the answer is negative.

steps: Both moves go left. Add the absolute values: $5 + 8 = 13$.

blocks.title: The positive one is smaller
steps: $-14$ is farther from $0$, so the sum is negative.

blocks.html: You can add any signed numbers. Subtracting turns out to be adding in disguise.
Subtracting a number is the same as adding its opposite: $$a - b = a + (-b)$$ So $3 - (-5) = 3 + 5 = 8$, and $-4 - 6 = -4 + (-6) = -10$.

Subtraction asks "how far from $b$ to $a$?" or "what do I add to $b$ to get $a$?" For $3 - (-5)$: from $-5$ to $3$ is 8 steps right, so the answer is $8$. With counters: to take 5 negative counters away from 3 positive ones, first add 5 zero pairs (that changes nothing), then remove the 5 negatives. Eight positives are left. Taking away a negative leaves you with more.

blocks.name: integerline
blocks.cap: $3 - (-5)$ is the same move as $3 + 5$: it goes right, the opposite way from adding $-5$.

blocks.name: counters
blocks.cap: Try "Take away −1" five times. Each time, the counters ask for a zero pair first. You end with 8 positive counters.

blocks.title: A temperature difference
blocks.q: The high was $-2^\circ$F and the low was $-9^\circ$F. How much warmer was the high?
steps: Check on a thermometer: from $-9$ up to $-2$ is 7 degrees ✓.

blocks.html: Treating "minus a negative" like "minus a positive," so that $3 - (-5)$ becomes $-2$. Remember the two changes: the minus sign becomes plus, and $-5$ becomes $5$. Check: subtraction undoes addition, so $8 + (-5)$ should give back $3$ ✓.

blocks.html: The absolute value of a number is its distance from $0$. With subtraction you can find the distance between any two numbers.
The distance between $a$ and $b$ on a number line is $|a - b|$. Subtracting in either order works, because $|a - b| = |b - a|$.

$a - b$ tells how far you move to get from $b$ to $a$, and its sign tells the direction. A distance has no direction, so we drop the sign with the absolute value. When the numbers are on opposite sides of $0$, you can also add their distances from $0$.

blocks.html: Multiplying by a whole number is repeated adding: $3 \times (-4)$ means three groups of $-4$, so $(-4) + (-4) + (-4) = -12$. But what could $(-3) \times (-4)$ mean? Nobody can make "negative three groups." A pattern answers the question.

Multiply the absolute values. The product is positive when the signs are the same and negative when they are different. With more factors, an even number of negative signs gives a positive product; an odd number gives a negative one.

Look at the pattern: $3 \times (-4) = -12$, $2 \times (-4) = -8$, $1 \times (-4) = -4$, $0 \times (-4) = 0$. Each time the first factor goes down by 1, we take away one group of $-4$, and the product goes up by 4. Keep the pattern going: $(-1) \times (-4) = 4$ and $(-2) \times (-4) = 8$.
The distributive property says the same thing: $$0 = (-1) \times (4 + (-4)) = (-1)(4) + (-1)(-4) = -4 + (-1)(-4)$$ The only number that makes this true is $(-1)(-4) = 4$.

Rational numbers follow the same properties as integers, including the distributive property that forced $(-1)(-1) = 1$. blocks.html: A fraction is a division: $\frac{3}{8}$ means $3 \div 8$. With long division you can turn any fraction into a decimal. Sometimes the division stops; sometimes it goes on forever, in a pattern.

Divide the numerator by the denominator. The decimal either terminates (the remainder reaches 0) or repeats (a block of digits repeats forever). A bar marks the repeating block: $\frac{2}{3} = 0.\overline{6}$ and $\frac{1}{6} = 0.1\overline{6}$.

When you divide by 6, every remainder is one of $0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5$. If a remainder is 0, the division ends. If not, a remainder must come back within a few steps, and from then on the division does exactly the same thing again, so the digits repeat. A fraction in lowest terms terminates exactly when its denominator has no prime factors except 2 and 5, the factors of 10.

blocks.html: In Grade 6 you saw that expressions can look different and still be equal, like $y + y + y$ and $3y$. Combining like terms is the everyday way to make an expression shorter without changing its value. The coefficients can be negative, fractions or decimals, so you will use signed-number addition too.

Like terms have exactly the same variable part, such as $3x$ and $-5x$, or $4$ and $-7$. Combine like terms by adding their coefficients: $3x + 5x = 8x$. Unlike terms, such as $3x$ and $2$, stay separate.

$3x + 5x$ is 3 groups of $x$ and 5 more groups of $x$: 8 groups in all. That is the distributive property, $3x + 5x = (3 + 5)x$. But $3x + 2$ is 3 groups of $x$ and 2 ones. Groups of $x$ and ones are different things, like cups and spoons, so they cannot be counted together.

Subtracting means adding the opposite, as with numbers. The opposite of a whole group is the opposite of each part: $-(x - 2)$ is $-1 \times (x - 2) = -x + 2$. If you took away only the $x$, you would have taken away less than the whole group.

blocks.html: An inequality like $3x - 4 > 11$ has many solutions. You can solve it almost exactly like a two-step equation, and graph the answer the way you graphed inequalities in Grade 6. There is one new rule.

Adding or subtracting slides both sides the same way, so their order stays the same. Multiplying by a negative number flips the number line around $0$: $2 < 5$, but $-2 > -5$, because $-2$ is to the right of $-5$. So after multiplying or dividing by a negative, the bigger side becomes the smaller side, and the sign must turn around to stay true.

blocks.html: In Grade 4 you learned that angles that fit together add. Some pairs of angles come up so often that they have names. Knowing them lets you find a missing angle without a protractor.

Complementary angles add to $90^\circ$ (they fill a right angle). Supplementary angles add to $180^\circ$ (they make a straight line). Vertical angles, across from each other where two lines cross, are equal. Angles all the way around a point add to $360^\circ$.

Why are vertical angles equal? Call the angles around a crossing $\angle 1$, $\angle 2$, $\angle 3$ and $\angle 4$, in order. $\angle 1$ and $\angle 2$ make a straight line, so $\angle 1 + \angle 2 = 180^\circ$. So do $\angle 2$ and $\angle 3$: $\angle 2 + \angle 3 = 180^\circ$. Both $\angle 1$ and $\angle 3$ are "$180^\circ$ minus $\angle 2$," so they are equal.

blocks.html: Sometimes the angles in a diagram are labeled with expressions like $(2x + 10)^\circ$. The angle facts give you an equation, and you know how to solve it.

Use the angle fact to write an equation: the parts of a right angle add to 90, angles on a line add to 180, angles around a point add to 360, and vertical angles are equal. Solve for $x$, then substitute to find each angle.

The labels describe the sizes of real angles. If two angles make a straight line, their sizes add to $180^\circ$ no matter how they are written, so the expressions must add to 180. That sentence is the equation.

blocks.html: You have sorted triangles by their sides and angles. Now a new question: given some measurements, can you build a triangle at all, and is there only one?

Sides: three lengths make a triangle only if the two shorter ones add to more than the longest. Then there is exactly one triangle. Angles: three angles fit a triangle only if they add to $180^\circ$. Then there are many triangles: the same shape in different sizes.

Lay the longest stick down. The other two are hinged at its ends and swing up. To make a corner, their free ends must meet above the long stick, and they can only reach each other if together they are longer than it. If they add to exactly the long side, they lie flat; if less, there is a gap. Angles alone cannot fix the size: a photo of a triangle, enlarged, has the same angles.

blocks.name: g7-sticks
blocks.cap: Change the stick lengths. The triangle closes only when the two shorter sticks add to more than the longest.

blocks.title: It works
blocks.q: Can 4 cm, 5 cm and 8 cm be the sides of a triangle?
steps: $9 > 8$, so yes. The three lengths fix the triangle: exactly one triangle.

blocks.title: It does not
blocks.q: Can 3 cm, 4 cm and 8 cm be the sides of a triangle?
steps: The short sides cannot reach each other: no triangle.

blocks.title: Range for the third side
blocks.q: Two sides of a triangle are 5 cm and 9 cm. What whole-number lengths can the third side have?
steps: It must be more than $9 - 5 = 4$, or the 5 and the third side could not reach past the 9.

blocks.html: Thinking any three lengths make a triangle, or that equal sums are enough ($3 + 5 = 8$ only lies flat). And three angles that add to $180^\circ$ do not give one triangle: they give a whole family of different sizes. Check sides by adding the two shortest; check angles by adding all three.

blocks.html: The distance around a circle is its circumference. Every circle, from a coin to a Ferris wheel, follows the same rule, and finding it needs only multiplying decimals.
$$C = \pi d = 2\pi r$$ The diameter $d$ goes across through the center; the radius $r$ is half of it. $\pi$ is about $3.14$ (or $\frac{22}{7}$).

All circles are the same shape: each is a scaled copy of every other. So the ratio of circumference to diameter is the same for all of them. Roll any circle along a line for one turn: it covers a little more than 3 diameters. That number is $\pi = 3.14159\ldots$; its digits go on forever without repeating, so $3.14$ is only an approximation.

blocks.name: circlepi
blocks.cap: Unroll the circle: one full turn is a little more than 3 diameters. Change the size; the ratio stays the same.

blocks.q: A circle has a radius of 7 cm. Find its circumference. Use $3.14$.

blocks.title: Working backward
blocks.q: A circular track is 47.1 m around. What is its diameter? Use $3.14$.

blocks.html: Using the radius where the formula needs the diameter ($3.14 \times 7 = 21.98$ instead of $43.96$). Check: the circumference is always a little more than 3 times the diameter. Another slip is thinking $\pi$ equals $3.14$ exactly; it only rounds to it.

blocks.html: You know the circumference of a circle and the area of a parallelogram. Cutting a circle into slices connects the two.
$$A = \pi r^2$$ Square the radius, then multiply by $\pi$. Area is measured in square units.

Cut a circle into many thin slices, like a pizza, and line them up, points up and down. They make a shape that is almost a parallelogram, and nearly a rectangle when the slices are thin. Its height is the radius $r$. Its length is half the circumference, $\frac{1}{2} \times 2\pi r = \pi r$, because half the crust is on top and half on the bottom. Area $=$ length $\times$ height $= \pi r \times r = \pi r^2$.

blocks.name: areaformulas
blocks.cap: Slice the circle and rearrange: the near-rectangle is $\pi r$ long and $r$ tall. More slices make it closer to a rectangle.

blocks.html: When you unfolded solids into nets, you saw that prisms and pyramids have flat faces. Now imagine slicing straight through a solid with a knife. The flat face you uncover is a cross-section.

A cross-section is the 2D shape where a flat plane cuts a solid. Each face the plane crosses gives the shape one side. A slice of a prism parallel to its base is a copy of the base; a slice of a pyramid parallel to its base is a smaller copy of the base.

The plane meets each face it crosses along a straight segment, and those segments join up into a polygon. A prism's side faces stand straight up, so a slice at any height matches the base exactly. A pyramid's faces lean in toward the top point, so slices shrink as they go up.

blocks.name: g7-slice
blocks.cap: Pick a solid and a direction, then move the plane. The gold shape is the cross-section; on the right it is shown face on.

blocks.title: A box, sliced parallel to the base
blocks.q: A box 6 in. long, 4 in. wide and 3 in. tall is sliced parallel to its base. What is the cross-section?
steps: The slice is a copy of the base: a 6 in. by 4 in. rectangle.
Its area is $6 \times 4 = 24$ square inches, at any height.

blocks.title: A pyramid, sliced through the top
blocks.q: A square pyramid is sliced straight down through its top point, parallel to one edge of the base. What is the cross-section?
steps: The slice crosses the base along a segment and passes through the top point.
So it has a flat bottom and a top corner: a triangle.

blocks.title: A cube with a corner cut off
blocks.q: A plane cuts the three edges that meet at one corner of a cube. What is the cross-section?
steps: The plane crosses three faces near that corner.
Three faces give three sides: a triangle. (If the three cuts are the same distance from the corner, all three sides are equal.)

blocks.html: You can find the area of composite polygons and the surface area of a solid from its net. This lesson puts both to work on real shapes.

Area of a composite figure: split it into rectangles and triangles and add, or start with a big rectangle and subtract the missing piece. Surface area: add the areas of all the faces, which is the area of the net.
Area adds up when pieces do not overlap, so any way you cut a figure gives the same total. A solid's faces unfold into a flat net without overlapping, so the surface area is the area of that net.

blocks.html: You know that a box's volume is $V = lwh$, even with fractional edges. That rule is part of a bigger one that works for every prism, including prisms with triangle bases.
For any right prism, $V = Bh$. $B$ is the area of the base, the face that is the same all the way through the prism, and $h$ is the distance between the two bases.

Slice a prism into layers 1 unit thick, parallel to the base. Each layer is a copy of the base, so each holds $B$ cubic units. There are $h$ layers, so the volume is $B \times h$. For a box, the base is a rectangle, $B = lw$, and $V = lwh$ is the same rule.

blocks.html: A statistical question is often about a big group: all the students in a school, all the voters in a town. Asking everyone is usually too slow or too costly, so we ask a smaller group and use it to learn about the whole.

The whole group is the population; the part you study is a sample. In a random sample, every member of the population has the same chance to be chosen. Random samples tend to represent the population well. Samples chosen for convenience can be biased.

If some members are more likely to be picked, the sample leans toward them. Ask only your friends how much they like your favorite band, and the answers lean high. Ask people at a gym how often they exercise, and the answers lean high too. Random choice gives no group an edge, so the sample's mix is likely to be close to the population's mix.

blocks.title: Choosing a plan
blocks.q: A principal wants to know how 7th graders get to school. Which plan gives a random sample: (a) ask the students in the bike club, or (b) draw 50 names from a box holding every 7th grader's name?
steps: In plan (b), every 7th grader has the same chance to be drawn.
Plan (a) leans toward students who bike.

blocks.title: Big but biased
blocks.q: A website poll gets 5,000 answers, and 85% say they like video games. Does this show that 85% of all people like video games?
steps: The people who answered chose to visit that site and to reply.
They are likely to be more interested in video games than other people, so the sample is biased.
A large biased sample is still biased.

blocks.title: In a factory
blocks.q: An inspector checks light bulbs for defects. Should she test the first 50 bulbs made in the morning, or 50 bulbs picked at random times through the day?
steps: The machine could change during the day, so the morning bulbs may not be typical.
Bulbs picked at random times give every bulb the same chance.

blocks.html: Trusting a sample because it is large. Size helps only when the sample is random. A huge sample of volunteers or friends can be far off. Ask first: did every member of the population have the same chance to be chosen?

blocks.html: A random sample is like a small copy of the population. So the fraction of the sample with some feature is a good estimate for the population. Turning that into a number is solving a proportion.

Use the sample's proportion (or its mean) for the whole population: $$\frac{\text{part of sample}}{\text{sample size}} = \frac{\text{part of population}}{\text{population size}}$$ Different random samples give somewhat different results. Larger samples vary less.

A random sample gives every member the same chance, so on average it has the same mix as the population. Any single sample can be a bit off, the way 10 coin flips rarely give exactly 5 heads. Taking several samples shows how much the estimates wobble.

blocks.name: sampling
blocks.cap: Each sample is 20 coin flips, and the dot is its proportion of heads. Samples vary, but they gather around $0.5$. Try larger samples: the spread shrinks.

blocks.title: Estimating a count
blocks.q: In a random sample of 50 students, 18 prefer an afternoon recess. The school has 600 students. About how many prefer it?

blocks.title: Combining samples
blocks.q: Three random samples of 40 students had 12, 15 and 9 students who play an instrument. Estimate the percent of all students who do.
steps: The samples differ, which is normal. Combine them: $12 + 15 + 9 = 36$ out of $120$.

blocks.title: Using a mean
blocks.q: A random sample of families in a town has a mean of 1.6 pets per family. There are 450 families. Estimate the total number of pets.

blocks.html: Expecting every sample to give the same answer, and deciding a sample is "wrong" when it differs from another. Random samples vary. Their results cluster around the true value, and with more or bigger samples the estimate gets steadier.

blocks.html: You can describe a distribution by its center and spread, and measure spread with the mean absolute deviation (MAD). To compare two groups, you need both.

Compare the centers relative to the spread: divide the difference of the means by the MAD (or the difference of the medians by the IQR). A gap of about 2 or more MADs means the groups are clearly different. A gap well under 1 MAD means the groups overlap a lot.

A difference of 3 points means a lot if each group's scores barely vary, and very little if scores spread over 30 points. Dividing by the spread measures the gap in "typical distances from the mean." When the gap is many of those, most of one group is above most of the other.

blocks.name: boxplot
blocks.cap: Quiz scores for two classes. The means are 70 and 78, and both MADs are about 4: the centers are about 2 MADs apart, and the boxes (the middle halves) do not overlap.

blocks.title: Clearly different
blocks.q: Plants with fertilizer A have a mean height of 64 cm; with fertilizer B, 72 cm. Both groups have a MAD of 4 cm. How different are they?
steps: Two MADs apart: the groups overlap only a little, so fertilizer B plants are clearly taller.

blocks.title: A lot of overlap
blocks.q: Two teams' jump distances have means of 70 and 72 inches. Both have a MAD of 6 inches. How different are they?
steps: Only a third of a MAD: the groups overlap a lot, and the difference may be ordinary variation.
blocks.a: About $\frac{1}{3}$ MAD apart: lots of overlap

blocks.title: With medians
blocks.q: Two box plots have medians of 40 and 52, and both IQRs are 12. How many IQRs apart are the medians?
steps: $12 \div 12 = 1$ IQR. That is a moderate gap: the groups still overlap some, so the difference is worth noticing but is not as clear as a gap of 2 or more.

blocks.html: Calling two groups different because their means are different. Every two groups have slightly different means. Always compare the gap with the spread: divide by the MAD and look at how much the dot plots or box plots overlap.

blocks.html: How likely is rain tomorrow? Rolling a 6? Probability puts a number on chance. Like a percent, it can be written as a fraction, a decimal or a percent.
A probability is a number from $0$ to $1$. $0$ means impossible, $1$ means certain, and $\frac{1}{2}$ means as likely as not. Numbers near $0$ are unlikely; numbers near $1$ are likely.

A probability tells what fraction of the time an event happens in the long run. An event that never happens has a fraction of $0$; one that always happens has a fraction of $1$; one that happens half the time has $\frac{1}{2}$. Nothing can happen less than never or more than always, so a probability is never below $0$ or above $1$ (above $100\%$).

blocks.name: numberline
blocks.cap: The probability scale runs from $0$ (impossible) to $1$ (certain). Unlikely events sit near $0$, likely ones near $1$, and an even chance is $\frac{1}{2}$.

blocks.title: An impossible event
blocks.q: What is the probability of rolling a 7 on a number cube numbered 1 to 6?
steps: No face shows 7, so it can never happen.

blocks.title: Reading a probability
blocks.q: The chance of rain tomorrow is $0.85$. Describe it.
steps: Rain is likely, but not certain.

blocks.title: Not a probability
blocks.q: Which of these cannot be a probability: $0$, $\frac{3}{7}$, $1.2$, $45\%$?
steps: $1.2$ is more than $1$: more than "certain," which is impossible.

blocks.html: $\frac{1}{2}$, $0.5$ and $50\%$ are three names for the same probability. Use whichever is easiest to compare.

blocks.html: Where do probability numbers come from? When all the outcomes are equally likely, like the faces of a fair number cube, you can work the probability out by counting. It is a number on the probability scale.
If all outcomes are equally likely, $$P(\text{event}) = \frac{\text{number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{total number of outcomes}}$$

Equally likely outcomes share the total probability, $1$, equally. With 6 faces, each face gets $\frac{1}{6}$. An event that includes 3 of the faces gets 3 of those shares: $\frac{3}{6}$. This only works when the outcomes really are equally likely.

blocks.cap: Roll a fair number cube many times. Each face settles near $\frac{1}{6}$ of the rolls.

blocks.title: A number cube
blocks.q: What is the probability of rolling an even number on a fair number cube?

blocks.title: A bag of marbles
blocks.q: A bag has 3 red, 5 blue and 2 green marbles. What is the probability of picking blue?
steps: There are $3 + 5 + 2 = 10$ marbles, each equally likely.

blocks.title: Numbered cards
blocks.q: Cards numbered 1 to 20 are shuffled. What is the probability of drawing a multiple of 3?

blocks.html: Theoretical probability needs equally likely outcomes. For a paper cup that can land up, down or on its side, we cannot count our way to an answer. We can run an experiment.

$$\text{experimental probability} = \frac{\text{number of times the event happened}}{\text{number of trials}}$$ It changes from experiment to experiment. With many trials it tends to get close to the true probability.

Each trial is a small piece of evidence. With only a few trials, luck can push the fraction far from the truth. With many trials, the lucky streaks in both directions tend to balance out, so the fraction settles down. This is called the law of large numbers.

blocks.cap: Roll 10 times and look at the share of 6s, then roll 1000. The share wanders at first and settles near $\frac{1}{6} \approx 0.167$.

blocks.q: A player made 18 of her last 25 free throws. About how many of her next 100 would you expect her to make?

blocks.title: Expected and actual
blocks.q: A fair number cube is rolled 60 times. How many 6s do you expect? If it shows 13 sixes, is the cube unfair?
steps: 13 is close to 10. Differences like this happen by chance all the time, so 13 sixes is no reason to call the cube unfair.

blocks.html: Expecting exactly ten 6s in 60 rolls. Ten is what you expect on average; any one experiment will usually be a little above or below. Over thousands of rolls the fraction of 6s gets close to $\frac{1}{6}$, but the exact count still varies.

blocks.html: A probability model lists the possible outcomes and gives each one a probability. Some models come from equally likely outcomes; others come from experiments. Comparing a model with real results tells you whether to trust it.

In a uniform model, every outcome has the same probability. In other models, probabilities differ, and they can be estimated from data. All the probabilities in a model add to 1. A model predicts about (probability × trials) occurrences; results far from that, over many trials, suggest the model is wrong.

A model is a claim about how chance behaves. Small differences between the prediction and the data are normal, because results vary. But if a spinner with 4 "equal" parts lands on red 180 times in 400 spins instead of about 100, chance alone almost never does that: the parts are probably not equal.

blocks.name: dice
blocks.cap: The sum of two number cubes is a non-uniform model: 7 is the most likely sum ($\frac{6}{36}$) and 2 and 12 the least ($\frac{1}{36}$). The data settle onto the dashed model.

blocks.title: Does it fit?
blocks.q: A spinner has 4 equal parts, one red. In 400 spins, it lands on red 103 times. Does the data fit the model?
steps: 103 is close to 100, a normal amount of variation. The data fit the model.

blocks.title: It does not fit
blocks.q: Another "equal parts" spinner lands on red 180 times in 400 spins. Does it fit?

blocks.html: For a theoretical probability you need to count all the outcomes. With two or three steps, like flipping two coins, that takes an organized list.

The sample space is the list of all possible outcomes. Organize it with a list, a table, or a tree diagram. When each step has a fixed number of choices, multiply: a coin and a number cube give $2 \times 6 = 12$ outcomes.

A tree branches at every step. Each of the 2 coin branches splits into 6 number-cube branches, so there are $2 \times 6 = 12$ paths. Each path is one outcome. Order matters: "heads on the first coin, tails on the second" is a different path from "tails, then heads."

blocks.html: A compound event is made of two or more simple events, like "heads and a 6." With a sample space you can find its probability by counting, and multiplying fractions gives a shortcut.

For equally likely outcomes, $$P(\text{event}) = \frac{\text{favorable outcomes}}{\text{all outcomes in the sample space}}$$ When the events do not affect each other (independent events), $P(A \text{ and } B) = P(A) \times P(B)$.

Half of all coin flips are heads, and $\frac{1}{6}$ of those also come with a 6 on the number cube. A fraction of a fraction is a product: $\frac{1}{6}$ of $\frac{1}{2}$ is $\frac{1}{2} \times \frac{1}{6} = \frac{1}{12}$. The tree shows the same thing: multiply along a path.

blocks.html: Some probabilities are hard to count, like "how likely is it to collect all 3 prizes in 5 cereal boxes?" A simulation uses a simple random tool to act out the situation many times. It is an experiment that stands in for the real thing, built on compound events.

To simulate: (1) choose a random tool whose outcomes have the same probabilities as the real situation, (2) decide what counts as one trial and what counts as success, (3) run many trials, (4) estimate the probability as successes ÷ trials.

A good simulation behaves like the real situation, because the chances match. And with many trials, an experimental probability gets close to the true one. So the fraction of successful trials estimates the real probability, even when no one can count it directly.
